:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = (y - x)\,\mathbf{i} - (x + y )\,\mathbf{j}$ across the closed curve $C$ given by $\mathbf r(t) = 4\cos t\,\mathbf{i} + 4\sin t\,\mathbf{j}$ for $t \in [0,2\pi).$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = 4\cos t, \qquad
	y = 4\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =y-x=4(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t), \\ Q(x,y) & =-(x+y)=-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(4(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t))\cdot (4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-(-4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t))\cdot (-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{cos}^{2}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-16t{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-16(2\pi -0) \\  & =-32\pi \end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = xy\,\mathbf{i} + x^2\,\mathbf{j}$ across the ellipse $C$ with equation $9x^2 + y^2 = 9.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
\oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \oint\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x,
$$

where $\mathbf{n}$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ 

First, we write the equation of our curve as

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{1^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

The closed curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at the origin with horizontal and vertical semiaxes $1$ and $3,$ respectively. It can be parameterized in the counterclockwise direction as

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \cos{t}\,\mathbf{i} +3\sin{t}\,\mathbf{j},
\qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.
$$

Along the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = \cos t, \qquad
y = 3\sin t.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =xy=3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t, \\ Q(x,y) & ={x}^{2}={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡t, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos t, \textrm d u = -\sin t\,\textrm d t,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }10\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{1}10{u}^{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Flux of a Vector Field Over a Closed Curve in Cartesian Form

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
![](images/6e/6eebbc5ae9f548f5b00de9a12d454fa788884bf73ad46a1065eab0d26330a921.png)

The curve $C$ is given by $y = \dfrac14x^2$ from the point $\left(0,0\right)$ to the point $\left(4,4\right).$ Calculate the flux of the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y) = -2\,\mathbf{i} + x\,\mathbf{j}$ through $C,$ measured with respect to the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C,$ as shown above.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
If $\mathbf{F} = P\,\mathbf i + Q\,\mathbf j$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple curve, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $C$ measured with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ on $C$ is given by

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = \int\limits_{C}P\,\textrm d y - Q\,\textrm d x.
$$

To apply this formula, 

- the curve should be parameterized as $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b],$ and

- the unit normal vector $\mathbf n$ *must* be a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of the unit tangent vector $\mathbf T(t).$

Parameterizing the curve $C,$ we have

$$
x = t, \qquad
y = \dfrac{t^2}{4},
\qquad
t\in \left[0,4\right].
$$

 

This parameterization traverses the curve from the point $(0,0)$ to the point $(4,4).$ Therefore, $\mathbf n$ is indeed a $90^\circ$ clockwise rotation of $\mathbf T,$ so we can apply the above formula for the flux. 

![](images/2b/2b94e24344f600fc02ec5ecac6c1e0ee4c6a5450132753a0a5ac5fceaa9aa1fc.png)

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x,y) & =-2, \\ Q(x,y) & =x=t.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivatives of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ along the curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{t}^{2}}{4})=\frac{t}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{C}P\,\text{d}y-Q\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(P\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}-Q\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-2)\cdot (\frac{t}{2})-(t)\cdot (1)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}-2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{4} \\  & =-16-0 \\  & =-16\end{aligned}
$$
